newsitem.title: BELGIUM: NATO's Solana backs U.S. action in Iraq.
newsitem.headline: NATO's Solana backs U.S. action in Iraq.

text.p: NATO Secretary General Javier Solana came out firmly in support of U.S. action against Iraq on Tuesday, despite some hesitation among leading members of the Western alliance.
Solana said the U.S. attack on targets in Iraq was "a justified, measured and proportionate response" to violations of United Nation orders.
He called on Iraqi President Saddam Hussein to stop attacks in the region and comply with U.N. resolutions.
"Iraq has once again blatantly and gravely violated U.N. Security Council resolutions and mounted an agressive attack against civilians inside the exclusion zone in northern Iraq," Solana said.
"Against this background the U.S. action this morning was a justified, measured and proportionate reaction.

"I hope that this clear message will be heeded by Saddam Hussein and that he will immediately withdraw his forces from the area, stop any further brutal attacks, and comply fully with U.N resolutions."
The United States on Tuesday fired 27 cruise missiles at air defence targets in Iraq in retaliation for attacks by Baghdad on Kurds in northern Iraq.
Reaction from NATO member countries has been mixed.

Along with the United States, Britain and Germany expressed full backing for the action. France, however, withheld its support and Spain, where Solana was foreign minister in the previous Socialist government, said it wished Washington had held back.
Turkey, the only NATO member bordering Iraq, said it had tried very hard through diplomatic means to allay the need for the strike.
NATO as an organisation kept a low-profile during the 1991 Gulf War launched under U.N. auspices.

Although NATO members, notably the United States, France and Britain, were involved in the fighting, Washington was keen that NATO should be kept at a distance for fear the drive to remove Iraq from Kuwait should be seen as the West ganging up on an Arab country.
The alliance, however, provided significant assistance to U.S.-led forces in the form of coordination and back up.
